claims.claim: Organizing involves coordinating and allocating a firm's resources so that the firm can carry out its plans and achieve its goals; in plain terms, organizing arranges resources and tasks so plans can be carried out.

Organizing is one of the four key management functions — planning, organizing, leading, and controlling — and the organizing process has three steps: dividing work into jobs (division of labor), grouping jobs and employees (departmentalization), and assigning authority and responsibility.

An organization chart is a visual representation of the structured relationships among tasks and the people given authority to do those tasks; it shows who reports to whom, and the chain of command can be traced from the top of the chart down to the employees doing the work.
Dividing work into specialized jobs lets employees build greater skill at a particular task, which can lead to greater efficiency and consistency in production and other work activities.

Formal organizations have well-defined lines of authority, channels for information flow, and means of control; a clear chain of command makes clear who reports to whom, and under the unity of command principle everyone reports to and takes instructions from only one boss.

A manager's span of control is the number of employees the manager directly supervises; the optimal span depends on factors such as the nature of the task, the location of workers, the manager's ability to delegate, the amount of interaction and feedback required, and the skill and motivation of the workers.
Delegating authority makes employees accountable to their supervisor; accountability means responsibility for outcomes and moves upward in the organization.

Centralization is the degree to which formal authority is concentrated in one area or level of the organization, with top management making most of the key decisions; decentralization is pushing decision-making authority down the hierarchy so lower-level people make and implement more decisions, bringing benefits such as quicker decisions and risks such as costly mistakes by less experienced staff.

Structure should serve strategy: managers must first consider what kind of work needs to be done within the firm, and the best structure for a company depends on factors including its size, strategy, industry, and culture.

An organization chart is a snapshot of formal reporting relationships; real organizations also run on committees, temporary teams, and informal relationships, so the chart is best treated as a map rather than the territory.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How wide a manager's span of control should be
positions: OpenStax Introduction to Business notes spans ranging from as narrow as two or three employees to as wide as fifty or more, and lists five factors that determine the optimal span (task nature, worker location, delegation ability, interaction and feedback needs, worker skill and motivation).
OpenStax Principles of Management treats span of control as one of the core design questions — along with centralization and formalization — with no universal number.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents span of control as a judgment call shaped by the five factors, with no single right number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Attribution of the 'structure follows strategy' idea
positions: The dictum is widely attributed in management writing to business historian Alfred Chandler's 1962 book Strategy and Structure.

This lesson's research verified the general idea in textbook form — managers must first consider what work needs to be done, and the best structure depends on size, strategy, industry, and culture — without reaching a primary source for the Chandler attribution.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the general idea (structure follows strategy) and attributes its supporting claims to the verified OpenStax and Investopedia sources; it does not name Chandler as the originator.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether centralization or decentralization is better
positions: Centralization lets top managers develop a broad view of operations, exercise tight financial controls, and reduce redundancy, but can slow the response to customers and starve lower-level staff of decision-making practice.
Decentralization brings quicker decisions, more innovation, faster development of lower-level managers, and higher commitment, but risks costly mistakes when staff lack skill and training.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the choice as a trade-off that depends on organizational size, environment, and people, not as a universally better arrangement.
